Whenever we say a *people* or a *multitude* wills, hopes, or does something, we understand it as the *city* <note>original: civitas; here meaning the organized political state or commonwealth</note> which commands, wills, and acts through the will of *one* man, or through the concurring wills of *many* men, which cannot happen except within an assembly. However, whenever something is said to be done by a multitude of men, whether large or small, without the will of that man or assembly, it is said to have been done by the subject people; that is, by many individual citizens together. This does not proceed from a single will, but from the several wills of several men. These, being citizens and subjects, are not the *city*.

<margin>
*The beginning of a city is the right of the majority agreeing.*
</margin>

II. Next, it must be considered that every individual from the multitude (in order for the beginning of establishing a city to occur) must agree with the others that, in those matters proposed by anyone in the assembly, that which the majority <note>original: major pars; the greater part</note> wills shall be held as the will of all. For otherwise, there will be no will at all for a multitude of men whose dispositions and desires differ so diversely among themselves. But if anyone refuses to agree, the others will nonetheless establish the city among themselves <unclear>con</unclear> <note>the text continues on the next page to complete the word constituent, meaning they will establish or constitute it</note>

<summary>Hobbes distinguishes between the state as a single legal actor and a disorganized collection of individuals, arguing that a commonwealth begins when a multitude agrees to abide by the will of the majority.</summary>
<keywords>sovereignty, commonwealth, multitude, people, majority rule, social contract, political will</keywords>
